Multi-agent triage for
Power BI refresh failures

What each part is, what it did on a live run, and where the boundaries are. All screenshots are from live runs, not mock-ups.

project bi-request-triage model gpt-5.6-luna 9 / 9 scenarios passing live 371 offline tests captured 31 Aug 2026

A What it does

A Power BI refresh fails. The alert lands in a monitored mailbox. From there, no human is involved unless the system decides one should be.

A Triage agent reads the alert and works a fixed procedure: has this failure been seen before, is it a data problem, is it safe to retry. It consults a separate Data Quality agent before it is allowed to consider any fix. If — and only if — the failure is transient and the data is clean, it performs exactly one remediation and reports what it did.

Connecting a model to a refresh button is straightforward. The constraints are the substance: what stops it refreshing forty times during an outage, or doing something nobody asked for — and what it does when the right fix is bigger than it is allowed to make. Four of the seven runs below are about that.

Summary The model decides what to propose; a controller decides what is allowed to happen. They are separate by design.

B The flow

Every run follows the same path. The order is enforced, not suggested.

   email alert
        │
        ▼
   compute failure signature ──────▶ incident store  "seen this before?"
        │                                   │
        ▼                                   ▼
   TRIAGE AGENT  (Foundry) ◀────── known?  ──▶ notify · duplicate_suppressed
        │
        │   every step charged against the policy ledger before it runs
        │
        ├─▶ get_request_context
        ├─▶ get_known_incidents
        ├─▶ consult_data_quality_agent ──▶ DATA QUALITY AGENT  (Foundry)
        │        │                                  ▲
        │        │        deterministic scan ───────┘   (runs first, no model)
        │        ▼
        │   issue found? ──▶ write flag · notify · flagged_data_quality
        │        │
        │        no
        │        ▼
        ├─▶ get_dataset_refresh_history
        ├─▶ refresh_powerbi_dataset      ◀── 1 of 1 remediation permitted
        ├─▶ notify_teams
        └─▶ report_resolution
                 │
                 ▼
        validate the claim against the evidence
                 │
                 ▼
        persist EVERY outcome — including crashes and refusals
Why the scan runs before the model The duplicate counts come from a plain scan of the source table, with no model involved. The Data Quality agent interprets those numbers; it never produces them. That is what makes the finding identical on every run — and it means a model that contradicts the evidence loses.
Knowledge is retrieved, not pasted into the prompt A catalogue of documented Power BI failure modes sits alongside the agent. Only the entries whose triggers match the incoming error are injected — capped at three — so the catalogue can grow without every call paying for it.

Each entry answers the question that actually changes the decision: is a retry useful? “Credentials expired” and “capacity throttled” both surface as refresh failed, but retrying resolves one and merely wastes capacity on the other while delaying the person who could fix it.

The entry that earns its place most: Power BI disables a scheduled refresh after four consecutive failures. An automated retry loop trips that threshold and then goes quiet — the report is stale, and no further alert is raised because no further refresh is attempted. The playbook tells the agent to escalate at three.

Each piece below is a real object in the Foundry project, shown as it appears in the portal.

  • 1 Two separate agents. bi-data-quality and bi-triage are independent Foundry agents — separate instructions, separate identities, separately versioned. The triage agent reaches the other one through a tool call, which is what makes this a multi-agent system rather than one agent with a longer prompt.
  • 2 Versions are first-class. Each agent carries a version number that increments when its definition changes. This matters more than it looks: a registered agent does not pick up local prompt edits, so "which version is actually serving" is a real question with a real answer.

1
2
3
  • 1 A guardrail policy defined in source and applied by script. It enables hate, violence, jailbreak and — most importantly here — indirect attack detection.
  • 2 Scoped to a model. Guardrails attach to deployments and agents rather than living inside prompt text.
  • 3 Bound to gpt-5.6-luna, so it is in force for every call this system makes.
Why indirect-attack detection matters in this specific system This agent reads email — text written by someone outside your organisation. That is the standard vector for indirect prompt injection: instructions hidden in content the agent is asked to process. Foundry screens for it on every call and reports the result inline, so we can show that the check ran rather than assert that it did.

Guardrails are content filters, though. They do not decide whether an agent may refresh a dataset. That is a different problem, solved differently — see Native vs custom.

Everything else in the project

Model deployment

The reasoning engine behind both agents
Foundry native A single gpt-5.6-luna Global Standard deployment serves both agents. Note “API Key authentication is disabled” — every call in this system authenticates with Entra identity, so there is no key to leak, rotate, or find in a config file.

Traces

Per-run visibility, including failures
Foundry native Connecting an Application Insights resource turns on trace capture, filterable by duration, tokens in/out, estimated cost and status. D Agent identity

Each agent has its own identity in Microsoft Entra, created automatically. That determines what credential it holds, what it can reach, and who is accountable for it.

live directory read triage-demo identity --check-scope
  • 1 No secret exists. stored secrets: none (keys=0, passwords=0). The blueprint behind each agent holds zero keys and zero passwords; it authenticates with a federated credential instead. This is not a secret stored carefully — it is the absence of one, which is a different security property. Nothing here can be leaked, rotated late, or allowed to expire.
  • 2 A named human is accountable. sponsor is populated in Entra, and nobody typed it in — Foundry recorded it when the agent was created. When something goes wrong at 3am, the directory can answer “whose agent is this?”, which an app registration cannot.
  • 3 The agents that think hold nothing. Both reasoning agents show Graph permissions: none and no Azure roles. They read evidence and return a verdict; they cannot act. The controller holds exactly two Azure roles — write incidents, emit traces — and no Graph permissions at all. A component that cannot act cannot be talked into acting.
  • 4 The mailbox is a boundary, and it is tested. App-only mail permission is tenant-wide by default — we confirmed that the uncomfortable way during design, when a test app read the global administrator’s inbox. The mailbox scope rows show one mailbox granted and another explicitly denied. The controller refuses to start if it can read a mailbox it should not.
  • 5 The last panel is the app registration. One conventional app registration remains, with passwords=1, an expiry date, and no sponsor. It exists because mailbox access is the one door an agent identity cannot open yet: with the same token, Microsoft Graph’s directory endpoint returned 200 and the Exchange-backed mail endpoint returned 401. Showing it makes the contrast concrete rather than theoretical.

E Hosted deployment

The controller runs as a Foundry hosted agent: a container in your subscription, with no laptop involved.

One caveat on the trigger, tested rather than assumed. A Foundry routine is registered against this agent with a five-minute schedule, and the platform reports it as enabled and accepts manual dispatches. It has never actually invoked the agent. Re-checked on 2 September, six days after it was registered: still zero runs, a dispatch still returns an id while the container does nothing, and telemetry shows activity only in the hours somebody invoked the agent by hand — a five-minute cron would appear in every hour. Routines are in preview and this looks like a preview defect rather than a misconfiguration. Until it fires, anything needing a timer should call the agent's endpoint from a scheduler you already trust; the agent itself is unchanged either way, because the scheduled path and the interactive path are the same code.

deployed container · East US azd ai agent invoke bi-triage-controller
  • 1 This answer came from Azure, not from the machine running the command. The container authenticates as its own agent identity — no connection string, no key, nothing in a config file to protect.
  • 2 Against a genuinely broken dataset. The semantic model in the demo workspace points at a SQL host that does not resolve, so its refresh really does fail. The refresh history the agent reads is a real Power BI API response, not a fixture.
  • 3 It declined to retry, and said why. A credentials failure is not fixed by refreshing, so retrying would spend the single permitted remediation on an action that cannot work. The agent escalated instead.
ConcernHow it is handled
State surviving a restart Incidents persist to Azure Table Storage. This is not about history: it is how a second alert about a problem already being worked is recognised as a duplicate. A container that forgets on restart is licensed to act twice.
Being woken A Foundry routine on a cron schedule — declared, but disabled because it does not fire; drive it from your own scheduler. The same container also answers interactively in the Playground, running identical code — a demo path that differs from the production path eventually demonstrates something that does not exist.
Mail it should ignore A relevance filter, and it is a security control rather than housekeeping. An agent that triages every message is steerable by anyone who can send it mail. Unfiltered against a real mailbox it triaged security digests and crashed on several; it now reports Ignored 10 message(s) that were not Power BI refresh alerts.
Choice of model Measured, not assumed. Both candidates passed all nine scenarios; the chosen one was faster and required one fewer correction from the controller. See docs/model-selection.md.

1 Transient failure — resolved

A scheduled refresh timed out. The data is sound and the failure is isolated, so one retry is correct.

live run · gpt-5.6-luna scenario 1 — transient
  • 1 The known-issue check runs second, before anything else is considered. The failure is reduced to a signature — a hash of the error with GUIDs, timestamps and request IDs normalised out — and checked against the incident store. Only if it is new does the agent continue.
  • 2 The data quality handoff happens before any fix is contemplated. A separate agent returns a structured finding. Refreshing a report never fixes a data problem, so this question is settled first.
  • 3 History turns an assumption into evidence. Two prior refreshes completed and one failed, so “isolated, therefore safe to retry” is a conclusion drawn from data rather than a guess.
  • 4 One remediation. The refresh is triggered and verified. The policy ledger shows Remediation writes: 1 — that is a hard ceiling, not a tendency.
  • 5 The summary states what happened, not what was attempted. Report, error, action, outcome, timestamp, and the specific evidence behind the decision.

2 Data quality issue — flagged, not fixed

The refresh failed with a duplicate-key error that does not say which rows are at fault. The system answers that question, records it, and deliberately stops.

live run · gpt-5.6-luna scenario 2 — data quality
  • 1 Same handoff, different answer. The Data Quality agent returns has_issue=True with specifics.
  • 2 The numbers are exact, and they are reproducible. Four duplicate rows across two key groups on (well_id, production_date). The original email only said “duplicate values exist” — it did not say which rows, how many, or on what key. Run this again and you get the same four, because a scan produced them rather than a model.
  • 3 A row is written to the data quality flag table — affected table, issue type, counts, detail. This is the record a data steward picks up.
  • 4 No remediation is attempted, and the ledger confirms it. This is a decision, not a gap. Look at the data: two duplicate rows are byte-identical and two differ by a single value. Keeping the first, the last, or the maximum are three different business answers, and picking wrong silently corrupts a production table. Flagging is cheap and reversible; deduplicating is neither.

3 Duplicate alert — suppressed

During an outage the same alert arrives repeatedly. This is the deduplication that stops the system acting on each one, and announcing each one.

live run · gpt-5.6-luna scenario 2b — duplicate suppression
  • 1 Run 1 behaves exactly as before — flags the issue and notifies.
  • 2 Run 2 is a different email with the same failure. Different message id, different arrival time; the signature matches. known_related_issue=True.
  • 3 It stops early. Four tool calls instead of six. No second flag row, no second remediation, and the notification says “already tracked” rather than reporting it as new.
  • 4 One incident, occurrence count 2. Not two incidents. The queue a human reads stays readable during an outage, which is precisely when it matters.
  • 5 It is announced once, not once per occurrence. A third alert with the same signature is counted on the incident and posts nothing. The controller checks the incident before delivering, so this does not depend on the model choosing to stay quiet. Without it, a five-minute sweep over an unresolved alert posts a card every five minutes — which is the alert fatigue this is supposed to remove.

4 Second remediation — refused by policy

This run tests the write budget: the agent requests a second remediation after already using one.

live run · gpt-5.6-luna scenario 3 — policy refusal
  • 1 The first remediation is permitted and completes.
  • 2 A second is requested — and never executes. The limit is an integer in code, checked before dispatch. No wording change to any prompt can raise it, because no prompt is consulted.
  • 3 The refusal is handed back to the agent as data, not raised as an error. That is a deliberate choice: the agent can still notify a human. An agent that goes silent the moment it is blocked is worse than one that escalates.
  • 4 The run ends as needs_human, not as a false success, and the incident is flagged for investigation. Blocked attempts are recorded — the gap between what the agent wanted and what it was allowed to do is exactly the population you mine when deciding what to automate next.
What this rules out The failure mode everyone has heard about — an agent retrying a broken job forty times overnight because nothing was counting — is not mitigated here by careful prompt wording. It is arithmetically impossible: the budget is spent, and the next request is denied.

5 Action outside the allowlist

This run tests the allowlist: the agent requests delete_dataset, which is not a permitted action.

live run · gpt-5.6-luna scenario 4 — outside the allowlist
  • 1 delete_dataset is not on the allowlist, so it is never dispatched. There is no code path from the model's output to an unlisted action — the name is checked against the permitted set before anything is called.
  • 2 The agent recovers and completes correctly. A refusal does not have to mean a failed run; it adapts and performs the legitimate remediation.
  • 3 Attempted versus dispatched are counted separately. Eight actions requested, seven executed. The discrepancy is the point, so it is visible rather than silently dropped.
  • 4 The run does not end clean. The legitimate remediation still happened, but the controller downgrades the outcome and flags the incident for review. An agent asking for something outside its vocabulary is a signal — either it knows something the operator does not, or the instructions need work. Both warrant a look.
  • 5 Adding a capability is a code change and a review, not a prompt edit.

6 Approval granted

The same gateway failure on three consecutive mornings. Another refresh would reproduce it, so the fix is a gateway rebind — an action that requires approval.

This is the branch that matters most, and the one most systems skip. Most real failures are not safe to fix automatically. The valuable shape is not the agent fixes it — it is the agent works the problem, proposes a bounded fix, and stops. A person makes one decision instead of doing one investigation.

live run · gpt-5.6-luna scenario 5 — approval granted
  • 1 Three consecutive failures change the answer. The agent reads the history and concludes a retry would reproduce the fault, so it does not propose one.
  • 2 rebind_dataset_gateway is proposed, not performed. It is on the allowlist — and separately marked as requiring human authorisation, because it affects every dataset bound to that gateway, not just the one that is broken.
  • 3 The approval card states the blast radius. An approval request that hides the consequence is a rubber stamp with extra steps, so the impact line is generated from the action rather than written by the model.
  • 4 Approved — and only then does the action run. The remediation budget is charged at that moment, not when the agent asked.

7 Approval denied

Identical to the previous run up to the decision. This time the approver declines.

live run · gpt-5.6-luna scenario 6 — approval denied
  • 1 Declined, and never dispatched. The gateway rebind did not reach the Power BI client at all.
  • 2 The reason is the valuable artefact. “The standby gateway also serves the finance datasets, and it is close week.” That is context the agent could not have had, and it is now attached to the incident.
  • 3 Remediation writes: 0. A denial costs the run nothing. This is subtle and easy to get wrong — if declining spent the budget, one “no” would silently disarm the agent for the rest of the incident and the next legitimate fix would be refused for a reason nobody could see.
  • 4 The outcome is approval_denied, not needs_human. They are different facts and belong in different buckets. A denial is the highest-signal event the system produces: the agent proposed something a person judged wrong, which informs what to automate next — and what never to.
Everything that is not a clear yes is a no An approval is only honoured if it is explicit, matches the exact action and its arguments, has not expired, and has not already been used. A timeout, a transport error, a malformed reply, a mismatched fingerprint, or no approval channel configured at all are all treated the same way: not approved.

Silence never reads as consent. There is a test named for it.
Who actually answers The seven runs above use a scripted approver, because a rehearsal has to be reproducible and cannot wait on a person. Outside a scenario — a live mailbox sweep, or the agent invoked from Foundry — the real gate runs: it writes the request to a table, posts the card, and polls until somebody answers or it expires.

Two things can write that answer, and the agent cannot tell them apart: the card's buttons, and triage-demo approve / deny. The buttons are links rather than Action.Submit, because a card posted through an incoming webhook has no bot behind it — a submit button there renders a control that silently does nothing, which is worse than no button.

While the agent waits, the run's wall clock stops. Both limits default to 300 seconds, so charging the agent for a person's reading time would kill the run as timed_out at the moment the approval was granted.

The card keeps its buttons after it is answered. A link cannot alter the card it sits on, and a webhook cannot edit a message it already posted, so the agent posts a separate note saying who decided — and a second click is refused twice over, by the callback and again by the agent.
Why the gate is code, not prompt wording An agent instructed to ask first will usually ask. Usually is not a control. The check sits in front of dispatch, so an unapproved action is never executed regardless of what the model decided — and the agent cannot claim a refusal it never sought, because the controller verifies that too.

8 The schedule Power BI switched off

After four consecutive failures Power BI disables a refresh schedule and never re-enables it. The cause gets fixed; the model stays dark, and nothing says so.

live run · gpt-5.6-luna scenario 7 — schedule re-enabled under approval
  • 1 Two playbooks match, and both say a retry will not help. Retrying a model whose schedule is switched off achieves nothing — the run succeeds and the model is still not on a schedule.
  • 2 The agent reads the schedule rather than inferring it. get_refresh_schedule returns whether it is actually enabled. A model that assumed it would be wrong exactly when it matters.
  • 3 Re-enabling is Tier 2, so it is gated. Turning a schedule back on means the model starts loading unattended again; if the underlying cause is not fixed, it fails four more times and switches off again. A person confirms the cause is gone.

9 The retry that would make it worse

The refresh failed because the capacity is throttled. The obvious response — retry — is the one response guaranteed to make the outage longer.

live run · gpt-5.6-luna scenario 8 — retry postponed, not attempted
  • 1 “Credentials expired” and “capacity throttled” both arrive as refresh failed. The playbook is what separates them, and it carries the field that changes the decision: whether a retry is useful.
  • 2 The outcome is deferred_retry. A distinct terminal state, not a quiet success. It had to be added to the model’s tool schema as well as the code — the first live run reported resolved because the enum did not list it, and the controller downgraded it.
  • 3 A deferral blocks an immediate refresh. While the window is open the controller refuses one, so the agent cannot talk itself into the retry it just decided against.
Where the limit lives The backoff is bounded at three attempts and enforced in the controller, not in prompt wording. The agent cannot raise it, and neither can a differently worded alert.

10 The failures that never send an alert

Everything above starts with an email. The failures that reach a report are the ones that do not send one: the refresh reports success while the data never arrives, loses most of its rows, or quietly loses a column. Nobody is told, because as far as Power BI is concerned nothing went wrong.

detector · deterministic the same four steps verified live on 1 September
  • 1 The first sweep says nothing. It records what healthy looks like. A detector that reports “still fine” every quarter hour is one people filter, and a filtered detector is not a detector.
  • 2 One odd reading is suspected, not announced. Two scans must agree before anything is said. False positives are the failure mode that kills a detector, so the design spends a sweep to avoid them.
  • 3 Only disappearances count. Models gain columns constantly; reporting that would fire on ordinary development and get the whole thing switched off, taking the removal case with it.
  • 4 It goes quiet again by itself. The finding clears when the model does, without anyone acknowledging anything.
No model writes the query The DAX is generated from stored configuration and escaped, so a prompt injection in an alert email cannot turn a read-only detector into an arbitrary query engine against the finance model. The judgement is arithmetic, not inference: a model asked whether a 60% row drop is acceptable will sometimes say yes.
configuration what is watched, and whether it can watch anything
  • 1 The watermark is read through the relationship. dim_date[date], not a column on the fact table — a star schema holds a date key, and there is nothing on the fact to take a maximum of. Pointing the probe at the date dimension instead returns the end of the calendar, which on a real model was 2030 while the data stopped in 2024.
  • 2 Weekday-only feeds are not stale on a Sunday. Reporting that every weekend is how a detector earns a filter rule.
  • 3 Preflight fails a configuration that cannot detect anything. That is the dangerous state: it looks like monitoring and reports nothing, for ever. A probe with no ids, a duplicate name on one model, or a confirmation count of zero all fail the check rather than running quietly.

F Notifications

Every terminal outcome produces a notification: resolved, refused, escalated or denied.

live · Teams, demo tenant posted by the deployed agent
  • 1 This card was posted by the agent, not staged. It arrived in the channel over a Power Automate Workflows webhook, from the container running in Azure, at the end of a real run.
  • 2 It carries the evidence, not just the verdict. Report, error, action taken, outcome and the incident signature — enough for whoever picks it up to decide whether they agree, without opening a console.
  • 3 The reasoning is in the card. "Refresh history contained only two prior API failures (no scheduled runs), so schedule deactivation is not at risk." That distinction between API-triggered and scheduled failures is what makes the answer correct rather than plausible, and it is stated where a human can check it.
  • 4 It says what it did not do. "No further automated retry was attempted" — the agent stopped, and said so, rather than leaving the reader to infer it.
  • 5 Redaction happens before this leaves the process. The card is built from redacted text, so a connection string in an error message never reaches a channel with a wider audience than the system it came from.

Two cosmetic notes, so nobody is surprised on the day. The post shows as a Workflows bot rather than a custom name or icon — a limitation of the replacement for the retired Office 365 connectors, which Microsoft removed on 22 May 2026. The sender line also renders an unresolved Workflows placeholder rather than a display name. Both are properties of the delivery mechanism, not of the agent, and neither affects the content.

G Foundry features vs. custom code

Most components are platform features. The exception is the policy layer, which encodes your operating rules.

ComponentProvided byNotes
Agent hosting, versioning, identityFoundry Each agent gets its own managed identity and version history.
Model servingFoundry gpt-5.6-luna, Global Standard, Entra auth — API keys disabled.
Agent-to-agent handoffFoundry The triage agent invokes the data quality agent as a distinct, separately versioned agent.
Content safety / prompt injectionFoundry Guardrails, incl. indirect-attack detection, applied to the deployment.
Tracing, token and cost accountingFoundry Via a connected Application Insights resource.
EvaluationsFoundry Available on the agent; not yet wired in this build.
Scheduled / event triggersFoundry (Routines, preview) Not yet wired — see limitations.
Action budgets and allowlistWe wrote this Nothing native does it, and Microsoft's own guidance says enforcement belongs in your code.
Retrieved failure-mode knowledge baseWe wrote this Documented Power BI failure modes, injected only when the error matches. Sourced from public docs so the asset stays shareable.
Human-in-the-loop approvalWe wrote this Fail-closed, fingerprint-bound, expiring, single-use. Nothing native enforces it.
Failure signatures and dedupWe wrote this Business logic: what counts as “the same failure”.
Deterministic duplicate scanWe wrote this Deliberately not a model call.
The distinction that matters Guardrails decide what may be said. The policy ledger decides what may be done. Foundry ships the first and — correctly — leaves the second to you, because “one dataset refresh per incident” is a statement about your operations, not about AI safety in general. The documentation is explicit that tool-approval enforcement is the calling application's responsibility.

That split is a feature, not a shortfall. The platform handles the parts that are the same for everyone; the small amount of code we wrote is the part that is specific to how this organisation wants its BI estate treated.

H Limitations

What this build does not do, and what to resolve before depending on it.

Not yet wired

ItemStatusWhy it matters
Routine triggerRegistered, never fires A Foundry routine is declared in azure.yaml with a five-minute cron, and the platform reports it enabled — but it has never invoked the agent. Re-verified six days after registration. Preview defect, not misconfiguration; drive the agent from a scheduler you already trust. Routine enabled-state is not managed by azd deploy in either direction, so use azd ai routine disable and check the result.
Live mailbox ingestionConnected The hosted controller reads a real mailbox with app-only Graph Mail.Read, scoped to that one mailbox by an Exchange policy. The runs above use fixed sample messages so the walkthrough stays reproducible.
Live Power BI refreshBuilt, not connected The refresh client exists; these runs used a mock so the demo does not depend on a dataset being in a particular state. The read path is live: the silent-failure detector queries real semantic models, deliberately through a separate client that holds no ability to change anything.
Direct Lake modelsNot supported by the platform A Direct Lake model reaches OneLake as the caller, and Microsoft does not support app-only callers for that, so the detector cannot query one however much permission it holds. It reports a detector fault rather than claiming the data is wrong. Point the model’s OneLake connection at a fixed identity, or probe an import model.
Traces from API-driven runsIngestion lag App Insights is connected and the trace surface is live, but entries had not appeared at capture time. Verify before relying on it in a session.
Human-in-the-loop approvalBuilt Both branches demonstrated live. The Teams Adaptive Card gate is implemented; these runs used deterministic gates so the outcome is reproducible.

Things to know before production

Mailbox permission scope App-only Mail.Read is tenant-wide by default. We verified this directly: an app registration created to read one demo mailbox was able to read the global administrator's inbox. It must be constrained with an Exchange ApplicationAccessPolicy scoped to the single alerts mailbox. Unscoped, “an agent that reads the BI alerts inbox” is an agent that can read every mailbox in the organisation.
Posting to Teams is deliberately harder than reading mail Graph restricts app-only channel posting to migration scenarios, so an unattended agent cannot post as itself. Reading a mailbox unattended is straightforward; writing into a human conversation is not. The demo uses a Power Automate Workflows webhook — note that the older Office 365 connector webhooks were retired in May 2026 — and a bot is the production answer.
Preview surface and API churn Routines, agent-to-agent tooling and several adjacent features are in preview. During this build two breaking API details surfaced within a single afternoon: one route rejects a query-string API version in favour of a path segment, and an agent property was replaced by agent_reference. Pin versions and re-verify before any session that matters.
Effort, for calibration The agents were roughly a day. The surrounding work — identity, permissions, provisioning, the trigger — was most of the effort. That is worth stating plainly, and it is the most useful thing to take from this document. A production-grade equivalent is weeks, and most of those weeks are not agent work: per-tenant budgets, secret handling at every boundary, a durable incident store, alerting, replay-based regression testing, and the human-approval branch above.
Scenario runs captured 28 August 2026 against Foundry project bi-request-triage (bitriage-foundry-eus, East US) on gpt-5.6-luna; the Teams post 31 August 2026. All nine scenarios passed against the live service; The offline suite passes with no tenant. Sample data is synthetic.
